title: When Success Misleads, 4 Leadership Books on Failure
author: William Meller
summary: William Meller opens with Dietrich Dörner's simulation in which an executive digs wells for the fictional Moro people and unintentionally causes a famine, to show that people who run complex systems fail for simple, predictable reasons. He then reads four books, written by non-managers between 1953 and 1998, as looking at failure at four scales. Dörner's The Logic of Failure studies the decider's head: unclear goals, fixing only visible defects, linear projection, and rarely checking results. Isaiah Berlin's hedgehog and fox essay, tested by Tetlock, suggests single big ideas predict worse than many small ones. Jackall's Moral Mazes shows how corporate hierarchy teaches that what is right is what the boss wants. James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State shows how making the world legible and countable, as with Prussian forests, produces fragile systems. Meller closes by noting that long runs of good results say nothing about what comes next.
points: Dörner's simulations show repeated errors: acting without clear goals, treating systems as loose parts, projecting in straight lines, and rarely checking the effects of one's own measures.
People protect their sense of competence, so someone who never examines the results of a decision can go on believing the problem was solved.
Berlin's hedgehog and fox distinction, tested by Tetlock, points to foxes with many small ideas predicting better than hedgehogs with one big idea.
Jackall's Moral Mazes finds that in large corporations what is right is what the person above you wants, and public talk of virtue need not connect to daily rules.

Scott's Seeing Like a State shows how making a forest or society easy to count discards local knowledge and produces fragile systems, and Dörner's executives succeeded through strategic flexibility rather than extra knowledge.
quotes: People who run complex systems tend to fail for simple and predictable reasons, and carelessness is rarely the explanation.
They treat the system like a pile of loose parts that can be moved one at a time, so they miss the side effect and the effect that takes time to arrive.
Someone who never looks at the result of a decision can keep believing the problem was solved.

In one experiment Dörner cites, participants checked between 30% and 50% of their own measures, and after an unexpected crisis (exactly when checking would make more sense) they checked less than 10%.
Those who think like hedgehogs, with one big idea, predicted worse than those who think like foxes (and both groups often lost to formal models).
What is right in the corporation is what the guy above you wants from you.
For Jackall, a company’s public talk of virtue has no necessary connection to the rules its managers follow day to day.
Scott calls this effort to make the world easy to count and control legibility
The Moros lived better for 10 years before the famine, and the Prussian forest paid off for almost 100 before it got sick. In both cases, a long run of good results said nothing about what came next.
